newsitem.title: USA: MWRA outlook revised to positive from stable - S&P.
newsitem.headline: MWRA outlook revised to positive from stable - S&P.

text.p: NEW YORK, Oct 17 - Standard & Poor's today has assigned its single-A' rating to Massachusetts Water Resources Authority's (MWRA) $150 million general revenue bonds series 1996A, which are scheduled to sell Oct. 22, 1996.

At the same time, Standard & Poor's has revised its outlook on the authority's bonds to positive from stable and has affirmed its single-A' rating on MWRA'S $2.63 billion parity debt and its A-1'-plus rating on $350 million commercial paper.
The single-A' rating reflects the following strengths:

-- The outlook change to positive reflects the substantial completion (86%) of the single largest project ($3.6 billion) related to the Boston Harbor cleanup -- The Deer Island Wastewater Treatment Plant. This limits the potential for increased project costs and allows for more realistic assumptions of future revenue requirements;
-- Continued progress of financing the construction of mandated projects at lower-than-anticipated costs due to strong management and very fortuitous inflation and interest-rate environments;
-- Still high, but lower-than-expected, retail rate needs;
-- The positive fiscal and political effects engendered by legislative action, including a direct debt service subsidy for sewer and water projects, and local tax-raising flexibility; and
-- The fiscally strong Boston Water & Sewer Commission (rated single- A'), which accounts for 33% of the authority's revenues.
These strengths are offset by the following risks:
-- MWRA is projecting substantial average annual rate increases of a maximum of 11% per year through 2002. This comes at a time when rates have not significantly been raised since 1993.
-- Uncertainty over the precise costs of constructing the water filtration plant and the MetroWest water supply tunnel.
-- Transitional issues relating to MWRA's establishment of a positive track record in operating the Deer Island facility.

MWRA's ongoing strengths include very strong collection enforcement mechanisms that have limited the impact of some local communities' fiscal weakening, and proactive and beneficial federal court oversight of mandated projects.

Standard & Poor's remains concerned about the rates that need to be absorbed by communities and their retail customers because of MWRA's still large and mostly mandated capital program, of which, $2.7 billion is projected to be spent through 2003. Although the much-feared $100 per month water and sewer bill will not be seen by ratepayers in this decade, Boston area rates will remain among the highest in the nation, relative to similarly sized communities.

MWRA's rating could be raised to single-A'-plus over the next one to three years provided continued positive progress in the capital program. This would include beginning the construction of the water system capital projects, successful implementation of future rate increases, no material deterioration in the credit quality of the 61 communities served, and the establishment of a successful track record in operating the Deer Island facility, Standard & Poor's said.
